```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(csvschema)
```

A CSV is the most portable data format there is and the most forgetful: open it
in a spreadsheet, a database loader, or another language and the types, factor
levels, and missing-value codes are gone. `csvschema` writes a CSV that carries
its own schema *inside ordinary data columns*, so the file is still a plain CSV
everywhere, but this package can rebuild the schema when it reads the file back
--- even after the file has been sorted, filtered, re-encoded, or passed through
a spreadsheet.

## Write and read

The package ships `dg_states`, a 50-row table of US state facts whose columns
cover every supported class: a factor (`region`), logicals (`south`, `west`),
an integer (`motto_year`), several doubles, and free text with non-ASCII
characters (`motto`).

```{r}
str(dg_states[, c("state", "region", "south", "motto_year", "motto")])
```

Write it with `cs_write()`:

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
cs_write(dg_states, path, verbose = FALSE)
```

The result is an ordinary CSV. The only difference from a plain export is two
extra character columns, `_schema` and `_canary`, whose cells hold short ASCII
tokens:

```{r}
raw <- read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
setdiff(names(raw), names(dg_states))   # the added, ignorable meta columns
substr(raw[["_schema"]][1], 1, 70)      # one cell holds packet tokens
```

Read it back with `cs_read_csv()`. The schema is recovered from those tokens and
applied automatically:

```{r}
out <- cs_read_csv(path, verbose = FALSE)
str(out[, c("region", "south", "motto_year")])
```

`region` is a factor again, `south` is logical, and `motto_year` is an integer
--- none of which a plain `read.csv()` restores.

## The report

Every read attaches a report describing what was recovered and whether the data
survived intact. Fetch it with `cs_report()`:

```{r}
rep <- cs_report(out)
rep$status                 # schema recovery status
head(rep$canary, 4)        # per-variable canary verdicts
```

`status = "verified"` means the schema was recovered in full and its
whole-schema hash matched. The canary table reports, per variable, whether the
data itself is still intact (more on that in `vignette("corruption")`).

## Surviving row loss

The schema is repeated and striped across the rows, so it survives losing most
of them. Here we keep only 10 of the 50 rows and still recover the schema:

```{r}
few <- read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)[seq(1, 50, by = 5), ]
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(few, tmp, row.names = FALSE)

out2 <- cs_read_csv(tmp, verbose = FALSE)
cs_report(out2)$status
```

How many copies of each packet that takes is pure arithmetic:

```{r}
cs_copies(20, f = 0.2)   # copies needed to survive losing 80% of rows
```

## A sidecar, too

`cs_write(..., sidecar = TRUE)` also writes a Frictionless `datapackage.json`
beside the CSV. It is the canonical, human-editable, tool-standard copy of the
schema; the in-band packets are the copy that cannot get lost. Each carries a
hash of the other, so a reader can tell which is stale.

```{r}
dir <- tempfile(); dir.create(dir)
csv <- file.path(dir, "states.csv")
cs_write(dg_states, csv, sidecar = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
list.files(dir)
```
